Recently, it has been brought to my attention the importance of having a retirement plan that is crafted with one spouse being a homemaker in mind.

I have been warned that it is unpleasant to spend your 50s and 60s working full-time to build up social security. Working because you want to is different from working because you have to. It is a very real possibility that you will outlive your husband by a decade and if you have things like an unpaid mortgage, you are at a serious risk of becoming homeless.

One suggestion made to me is to avoid buying a retirement home and prioritize getting a home, paying it off and maintaining it. That permanent home could be an RV or trailer, even. Just make sure it's paid for.

Another suggestion made to me is to hoard jewelry, coins and bullion. Even a poor family can afford to purchase the occasional silver coin. These things can also be easily passed out as inheritance without the prying eyes of the taxman.

Homemakers need retirement plans, too. Start working on your today.

Step 1: Live within your means from a young age. You'll never get ahead being a debt slave with a fancy car and using home equity to pay for vacations or granite countertops.

Step 2: Be self-sufficient whenever possible (You can learn just about anything from YouTube videos). Instead of paying a mechanic $1000 for a brake job, spend $75-300 on parts, and do it yourself. Use the $700+ saved money to make extra principal payments.

Note: I'm not a fan of tax advantaged stuff like 401k plans or mortgage interest deductions. Anything the government has to bribe you to do with tax breaks is usually not in your best interests.

Step 3: Once you're out of debt, don't chase hot investments. Choose five or more general categories like cash, real estate, precious metals, different categories of stocks, etc. Try to pick things that move in opposite directions, like home builder stocks and gold.

When you have your five categories invest the same amount in each, and every three months or so, try to rebalance as they move against each other. You can sell off some of the high performers to buy a few more low performers.

Simple example with only two categories: When the dollar drops your $10k in gold may go up to $11k, so you sell an ounce to buy something like a home builder stock which has fallen a bit. When the dollar goes back up, the stock rises to $13k, so you sell the extra stock to buy two ounces of gold.

This is the opposite of chasing hot stocks, and it's the safe way of cashing in gains as things move against each other. The more categories you have, the safer it is, and you don't even need to know why they're doing it or guess about how things will move. You just take advantage when they do, and adjust to keep each category worth the same as the others.
